title: Derivatives Fundamentals
summary: Forwards, futures and options: how they work, what they cost, and how their risk is measured. Education only.

modules.title: Forward Contracts and Counterparty Risk
modules.subject: Forwards
modules.learned: Describe a forward contract, estimate its price from spot and financing, and explain its counterparty risk and hedge trade-off.

check.q: A business fixes a future fuel cost with a forward. The spot price later falls. What is the business's position?
options: It is locked into the agreed price, so it gives up the benefit of the fall
It gains automatically, because the agreed price is always the best
The forward is cancelled when prices move
It must pay the difference to a government fund
check.explanation: A forward removes price risk in both directions. The business trades the chance of a benefit for certainty of cost.

modules.title: Futures, Margin and Daily Settlement
modules.subject: Futures
modules.learned: Explain standardisation and clearing, distinguish the margins, calculate daily settlement, and describe basis risk.

check.q: A long futures position loses 1,000 on Monday and gains 400 on Tuesday. What is the net variation margin over the two days?
options: A gain of 1,400
A loss of 600
No movement, because futures settle only at expiry
A gain of 600
check.explanation: Variation margin is settled daily. Minus 1,000 plus 400 gives a net loss of 600.

modules.title: Options: Rights, Premium and Breakeven
modules.subject: Options
modules.learned: Explain calls and puts, calculate intrinsic and time value, and find the breakeven and maximum loss of a long option.

check.q: A call has a strike of 50 and a premium of 3. What is the breakeven at expiry for the buyer?
check.explanation: The breakeven of a long call is the strike plus the premium, so 50 plus 3 is 53.

modules.title: Covered Calls and Protective Puts
modules.subject: Option strategies
modules.learned: Read the payoff of a covered call and a protective put, and calculate the cap or floor each creates.

check.q: A holder owns a stock bought at 40 and buys a put with a strike of 38 for a premium of 1. What is the floor per share for the protected position?
check.explanation: The floor is the put strike minus the premium, here 38 minus 1, which is 37 per share.

modules.title: Option Pricing and the Greeks
modules.subject: Pricing and sensitivities
modules.learned: List the inputs to an option price, describe delta, gamma, theta and vega, and explain the limits of option models.

check.q: Which Greek measures how fast delta changes as the spot price moves?
options: Gamma
Theta
Delta
Vega
check.explanation: Gamma measures the rate of change of delta, which matters for positions near the strike or near expiry.

modules.title: Derivatives Risk, Limits and Escalation
modules.subject: Derivatives risk
modules.learned: Name the sources of derivative risk, measure hedge effectiveness and residual risk, and escalate limit breaches.

check.q: A desk has a notional exposure of 5 million and a deposit of 500,000. Which figure should test its exposure limit?
options: The 500,000 deposit, because it is the cash committed
The 5 million notional, or its delta-equivalent, because losses scale with exposure
The average of the two figures
Neither, because limits are never set on exposure
check.explanation: Losses scale with exposure, so the limit must test the exposure, not only the deposit.

questions.q: What is a forward contract?
options: A private agreement to buy or sell an asset at a set price on a future date
An exchange-traded contract with daily settlement
An option that the buyer may decline
A loan secured on the asset

questions.q: Why is a forward usually exposed to counterparty risk?
options: Because forwards are always guaranteed by the exchange
Because it is private and not usually cleared, so each side depends on the other
Because forward prices are set by the government
Because the contract has no delivery date

questions.q: Roughly how is a forward price estimated?
options: Spot price minus the expected rise in price
The average of the last ten spot prices
Spot price plus the cost of financing until delivery, less any income the asset pays
The strike price of the nearest option

questions.q: What is arbitrage in the context of forward pricing?
options: Guessing where the spot price will move next year
A fee paid to the clearing house
The right to cancel a forward at any time
Locking a risk-free gain when a forward price is far from spot plus financing

questions.q: A business hedges a future cost with a forward. What does the hedge give up?
options: The benefit of a price fall, in exchange for certainty of the cost
All of its counterparty risk
Its right to buy the asset at spot
Any need for a budget

questions.q: What distinguishes a futures contract from a forward?
options: It is settled once, at expiry, with no cash in between
It is standardised and exchange-traded, and cleared through a clearing house
It has no delivery date
It is negotiated privately with each buyer

questions.q: What does a clearing house do?
options: It sets the spot price of the asset
It guarantees a profit for every trade
It stands between buyers and sellers and reduces each party's default risk
It lends money to clients at a fixed rate

questions.q: What is variation margin?
options: The deposit needed to open a position
The fee paid to the broker each month
The interest earned on the deposit
The daily gain or loss on a futures position, settled in cash

questions.q: A short futures position is used to hedge which exposure?
options: A long physical stock that will be sold later
A future purchase of the commodity
A loan taken to buy shares
A currency position that is already short

questions.q: What is basis risk?
options: The risk that the broker charges a higher margin
The risk that the spot-futures difference changes, so the hedge is not perfect
The risk that the contract expires on a holiday
The risk that the futures market is closed

questions.q: What right does a call option give its buyer?
options: The obligation to buy the asset at the strike
The right to sell the asset at the strike
The right, not the obligation, to buy the asset at the strike
The right to receive the premium

questions.q: What is the buyer's maximum loss on an option?
options: Unlimited, for any call
The strike price
The difference between strike and spot
The premium paid

questions.q: A call has a strike of 50, a premium of 3 and a spot of 52. What is its intrinsic value?
A put has a strike of 40 and a premium of 2. What is its breakeven at expiry for the buyer?
Who carries the potentially large loss in an option contract?
options: The buyer of a call, whose premium can rise without limit
The buyer of a put, because the strike can move
The seller, who takes the obligation and collects only the premium
Neither party, because options are guaranteed

questions.q: What does a covered call combine?
options: A long position in the asset with a long put
Two calls with different strikes and no asset
A short position in the asset with a long call
A long position in the asset with a short call on the same asset

questions.q: What does a covered call give up?
options: The upside above the call strike, in exchange for premium income
All of the asset's downside
The premium received
The right to sell the asset

questions.q: What does a protective put set under a long position?
options: A cap on the gain at the strike
A floor on the loss, with the premium as the cost of that floor
A guaranteed profit above the purchase price
A reduction in the asset's own risk to zero

questions.q: A stock is bought at 60 and a put with a strike of 55 is bought for a premium of 2. What is the floor per share?
What is a kink on a payoff diagram?
options: A point where the premium is paid
A point where the asset is delivered
A point where margin is called
A point where the slope changes, usually at a strike

questions.q: What is the main unknown input in option pricing?
options: Volatility, which is not directly observed
The strike, which is fixed in the contract
The expiry date, which is always known
The broker's commission

questions.q: A long call has a delta of 0.6. The underlying rises by 1. What happens approximately?
options: The call falls by 0.6
The call rises by about 0.6
The call rises by 1
The call does not change

questions.q: What does theta measure for a long option holder?
options: The sensitivity to a change in the spot price
The sensitivity to interest rates
The daily change in value from the passing of time, usually a cost
The change in the strike price

questions.q: What does vega measure?
options: The change in the premium over one day
The sensitivity to the strike price
The rate of change of delta
The sensitivity of the option's value to implied volatility

questions.q: In which year was the Black-Scholes model published?
Why must limits test exposure rather than only the deposit?
options: Because deposits are always larger than exposures
Because losses scale with the exposure, while the deposit is only the cash committed
Because the deposit is set by the regulator
Because exposure is never linked to losses

questions.q: What is residual risk?
options: The profit left after a hedge is closed
The margin returned at expiry
The part of an exposure that a hedge does not offset, which remains open
The premium refunded when a hedge is cancelled

questions.q: A desk passes its net delta limit late in the session. What should happen?
options: The breach waits until the next morning
The limit is raised to fit the position
The desk adds positions to hedge the breach
The breach is escalated the same day, with the cost and a plan recorded

questions.q: What should a stress test show that a normal limit does not?
options: The loss under large moves in spot, volatility or basis, when liquidity is weakest
The average daily profit of the desk
The number of trades placed in a month
The fees paid to the clearing house

questions.q: What is the purpose of a liquidity plan?
options: To guarantee that every position can be closed at the screen price
To show how positions would be reduced in stress, and how long it would take
To record the trader's emotions during the day
To raise the limit when markets are calm
